name: Jet peel (needle-free)

lead: A jet peel uses a pressurised stream of saline, oxygen or serum to treat skin and deliver products without needles. Clinics offer it as a hydration or glow treatment for a smoother, plumper look.

A handheld device propels a fine jet at the skin surface; providers say this lightly exfoliates and drives products in. A small registered comparison of a hydrating treatment and a jet peel for facial hydration (23 participants) is the only related research found, with no results available.

paras: It is done in a clinic session, usually described as low downtime, and often used before events.
No safety data specific to jet peel were found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Clinics offer it as a needle-free facial for hydration and a smoother look. A pressurised stream hydrates the skin surface and delivers products, giving plumper-looking skin. Little has been published on it.

lead: A jet peel is an aesthetic facial in which a handheld wand propels pressurised streams of saline, oxygen or a serum across the skin without needles. People book it for a fresher, smoother, more hydrated look, and clinics also use it as a way of working serums into the skin.[1][2]

Healthline describes the usual session as a wand that cleans the skin with oxygen and saline, followed by a custom serum, often containing hyaluronic acid, salicylic acid, glycolic acid, vitamin C or B vitamins, that the jet pushes into the skin. Claimed appearance benefits include smoother skin from exfoliation, a more even tone, softer-looking scars, deeper pore cleansing and a reduced look of wrinkles and sun damage.[2]

The technology descends from medical jet injectors, which deliver liquid through the skin under high pressure and have been used since the mid-twentieth century for mass vaccination and insulin.[3] Research specific to cosmetic jet peels is limited to one small registered comparison of a hydrating treatment and a jet peel for facial skin hydration.[1]
infobox: Hyaluronic acid, salicylic acid, glycolic acid, vitamin C, B vitamins [2]
About $125-159 per session in one example [2]

paras: Jet peel devices use a high-velocity jet of liquid or gas to treat the skin surface. Providers describe the method as a way of cleansing, lightly exfoliating and applying serums without needles, in short sessions without downtime.[2]
Healthline notes that, despite the name, a jet peel is a non-invasive facial rather than a chemical or laser peel, and that the serum is chosen by the provider to suit the person's skin goals.[2]

Needle-free jet injection predates cosmetic use. A fluid-injection device was presented to the Paris Academie Imperiale de Medecine in 1866, mid-1930s prototypes were inspired by accidental injuries from diesel injectors, and the Hypospray reached clinical use in 1947.[3]
Wikipedia's jet injector article describes injection into the skin layers by a piston-driven stream and does not discuss cosmetic applications.[3]

Providers recommend jet peels for fine lines, dull or dehydrated skin, congested pores and uneven tone, and some people repeat sessions every two to four weeks, though Healthline says recommendations on frequency are anecdotal.[2]

A 2024 paper in Skin Research and Technology reported on poly-d,l-lactic acid delivered by transdermal microjet for atrophic scars in Asian patients, a related needle-free delivery approach in aesthetics.[4]

Healthline lists redness, swelling, pain, pustules or cysts, enlarged lymph nodes and infection as possible side effects, with cellulitis rare, and says jet peels are not usually recommended during pregnancy.[2]

Medical jet injectors have a documented history of cross-contamination between users through splash-back and suck-back, including a hepatitis B outbreak at a 1980s weight-loss clinic and a 1988 podiatry clinic infection cluster; single-use or protected nozzles in modern devices address this concern.[3]
Healthline cites $125 to $159 per session or $300 to $435 for a three-session package, with insurance unlikely to cover it.[2]

One trial registration, NCT07793149, compares a hydrating treatment branded KIRA with jet peel for facial skin hydration and skin rejuvenation in 23 participants; it began in May 2026 and is listed as completed, without published results.[1] A 2024 study examined microjet delivery of poly-d,l-lactic acid for atrophic scars.[4] No other studies on cosmetic jet peel were found.

timeline.event: A fluid-injection device without a needle is presented in Paris.[3]
The Hypospray jet injector is introduced clinically.[3]
The US Department of Defense stops using multi-use jet injectors for mass vaccination.[3]
